{{Short description|Generalization in fractional calculus}} 

In [[mathematics]], the '''Caputo fractional derivative''', also called Caputo-type fractional derivative, is a generalization of derivatives for non-integer orders named after [[Michele Caputo]]. Caputo first defined this form of [[fractional derivative]] in 1967.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Diethelm |first=Kai |title=Fractional Differential Equations |date=2019 |chapter=General theory of Caputo-type fractional differential equations |pages=1–20 |doi=10.1515/9783110571660-001 |isbn=978-3-11-057166-0 |chapter-url=https://opus4.kobv.de/opus4-fhws/frontdoor/index/index/year/2023/docId/3212 |access-date=2023-08-10}}</ref>

== Motivation ==
The Caputo fractional derivative is motivated from the [[Riemann–Liouville integral|Riemann–Liouville fractional integral]]. Let <math display="inline">f</math> be continuous on <math>\left( 0,\, \infty \right)</math>, then the Riemann–Liouville fractional integral <math display="inline">{^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}}</math> states that

<math display="block">{_{0}^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] = \frac{1}{\Gamma\left( \alpha \right)} \cdot \int\limits_{0}^{x} \frac{f\left( t \right)}{\left( x - t \right)^{1 - \alpha}} \, \operatorname{d}t</math>

where <math display="inline">\Gamma\left( \cdot \right)</math> is the [[Gamma function]].

Let's define <math display="inline">\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha} := \frac{\operatorname{d}^{\alpha}}{\operatorname{d}x^{\alpha}}</math>, say that <math display="inline">\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha} \operatorname{D}_{x}^{\beta} = \operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha + \beta}</math> and that <math display="inline">\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha} = {^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}_{x}^{-\alpha}}</math> applies. If <math display="inline">\alpha = m + z \in \mathbb{R} \wedge m \in \mathbb{N}_{0} \wedge 0 < z < 1</math> then we could say <math display="inline">\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha} = \operatorname{D}_{x}^{m + z} = \operatorname{D}_{x}^{z + m} = \operatorname{D}_{x}^{z - 1 + 1 + m} = \operatorname{D}_{x}^{z - 1}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{1 + m} = {^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}}_{x}^{1 - z}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{1 + m}</math>. So if <math>f</math> is also <math>C^{m}\left( 0,\, \infty \right)</math>, then

<math display="block">{\operatorname{D}_{x}^{m + z}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] = \frac{1}{\Gamma\left( 1 - z \right)} \cdot \int\limits_{0}^{x} \frac{f^{\left( 1 + m \right)}\left( t \right)}{\left( x - t \right)^{z}} \, \operatorname{d}t.</math>

This is known as the Caputo-type fractional derivative, often written as <math display="inline">{ ^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}}_{x}^{\alpha}</math>.

== Definition ==
The first definition of the Caputo-type fractional derivative was given by Caputo as:

<math display="block">{^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{m + z}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] = \frac{1}{\Gamma\left( 1 - z \right)} \cdot \int\limits_{0}^{x} \frac{f^{\left( m + 1 \right)}\left( t \right)}{\left( x - t \right)^{z}} \, \operatorname{d}t</math>

where <math>C^{m}\left( 0,\, \infty \right)</math> and <math display="inline">m \in \mathbb{N}_{0} \wedge 0 < z < 1</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Caputo |first=Michele |date=1967 |title=Linear Models of Dissipation whose Q is almost Frequency Independent-II |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229523286 |journal=ResearchGate |volume=13 |issue=5 |pages=530|doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.1967.tb02303.x |doi-access=free |bibcode=1967GeoJ...13..529C }}</ref>

A popular equivalent definition is:

<math display="block">{^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] = \frac{1}{\Gamma\left( \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha \right)} \cdot \int\limits_{0}^{x} \frac{f^{\left( \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil \right)}\left( t \right)}{\left( x - t \right)^{\alpha + 1 - \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil}}\, \operatorname{d}t</math>

where <math display="inline">\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0} \setminus \mathbb{N}</math> and <math display="inline">\left\lceil \cdot \right\rceil</math> is the [[Floor and ceiling functions|ceiling function]]. This can be derived by substituting <math display="inline">\alpha = m + z</math> so that <math display="inline">\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil = m + 1</math> would apply and <math display="inline">\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil + z = \alpha + 1 </math> follows.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lazarević |first1=Mihailo |last2=Rapaić |first2=Milan Rade |last3=Šekara |first3=Tomislav |date=2014 |title=Introduction to Fractional Calculus with Brief Historical Background |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/312137269 |journal=ResearchGate |pages=8}}</ref>

Another popular equivalent definition is given by:

<math display="block">{^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] = \frac{1}{\Gamma\left( n - \alpha \right)} \cdot \int\limits_{0}^{x} \frac{f^{\left( n \right)}\left( t \right)}{\left( x - t \right)^{\alpha + 1 - n}}\, \operatorname{d}t</math>

where <math display="inline">n - 1 < \alpha < n \in \mathbb{N}. </math>.

The problem with these definitions is that they only allow arguments in <math display="inline">\left( 0,\, \infty \right)</math>. This can be fixed by replacing the lower integral limit with <math display="inline">a</math>: <math display="inline">{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] = \frac{1}{\Gamma\left( \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha \right)} \cdot \int\limits_{a}^{x} \frac{f^{\left( \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil \right)}\left( t \right)}{\left( x - t \right)^{\alpha + 1 - \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil}}\, \operatorname{d}t</math>. The new domain is <math display="inline">\left( a,\, \infty \right)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dimitrov |first1=Yuri |last2=Georgiev |first2=Slavi |last3=Todorov |first3=Venelin |date=2023 |title=Approximation of Caputo Fractional Derivative and Numerical Solutions of Fractional Differential Equations |journal=Fractal and Fractional|volume=7 |issue=10 |page=750 |doi=10.3390/fractalfract7100750 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Properties and theorems ==

=== Basic properties and theorems ===
A few basic properties are:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sikora |first=Beata |date=2023 |title=Remarks on the Caputo fractional derivative |url=https://minut.polsl.pl/articles/B-23-001.pdf |journal=Matematyka I Informatyka Na Uczelniach Technicznych |issue=5 |pages=78–79}}</ref>
{| class="wikitable"
|+A table of basic properties and theorems
!Properties
!<math>f\left( x \right)</math>
!<math>{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right]</math>
!Condition
|-
|Definition
|<math>f\left( x \right)</math>
|<math>f^{\left( \alpha \right)}\left( x \right) - f^{\left( \alpha \right)}\left( a \right)</math>
|
|-
|Linearity
|<math>b \cdot g\left( x \right) + c \cdot h\left( x \right)</math>
|<math>b \cdot {_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ g\left( x \right) \right] + c \cdot {_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ h\left( x \right) \right]</math>
|
|-
|Index law
|<math>\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\beta}</math>
|<math>{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha + \beta}}</math>
|<math>\beta \in \mathbb{Z}</math>
|-
|Semigroup property
|<math>{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\beta}}</math>
|<math>{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha + \beta}}</math>
|<math>\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil = \left\lceil \beta \right\rceil</math>
|}

==== Non-commutation ====
The index law does not always fulfill the property of commutation:

<math display="block">\operatorname{_{a}^{\text{C}}D}_{x}^{\alpha}\operatorname{_{a}^{\text{C}}D}_{x}^{\beta} = \operatorname{_{a}^{\text{C}}D}_{x}^{\alpha + \beta} \ne \operatorname{_{a}^{\text{C}}D}_{x}^{\beta}\operatorname{_{a}^{\text{C}}D}_{x}^{\alpha}</math>

where <math>\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0} \setminus \mathbb{N} \wedge \beta \in \mathbb{N}</math>.

==== Fractional Leibniz rule ====
The Leibniz rule for the Caputo fractional derivative is given by:

<math display="block">\operatorname{_{a}^{\text{C}}D}_{x}^{\alpha}\left[ g\left( x \right) \cdot h\left( x \right) \right] = \sum\limits_{k = 0}^{\infty}\left[ \binom{a}{k} \cdot g^{\left( k \right)}\left( x \right) \cdot \operatorname{_{a}^{\text{RL}}D}_{x}^{\alpha - k}\left[ h\left( x \right) \right] \right] -  \frac{\left( x - a \right)^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma\left( 1 - \alpha \right)} \cdot g\left( a \right) \cdot h\left( a \right)</math>

where <math display="inline">\binom{a}{b} = \frac{\Gamma\left( a + 1 \right)}{\Gamma\left( b + 1 \right) \cdot \Gamma\left( a - b + 1 \right)}</math> is the [[binomial coefficient]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Huseynov |first1=Ismail |last2=Ahmadova |first2=Arzu |last3=Mahmudov |first3=Nazim |date=2020 |title=Fractional Leibniz integral rules for Riemann-Liouville and Caputo fractional derivatives and their applications |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/347535345 |journal=ResearchGate |pages=1|arxiv=2012.11360 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |date=2024 |title=Binomial Coefficient |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/BinomialCoefficient.html |access-date=2024-05-20 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

=== Relation to other fractional differential operators ===
Caputo-type fractional derivative is closely related to the Riemann–Liouville fractional integral via its definition:

<math display="block">{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] = {_{a}^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}_{x}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha}}\left[ \operatorname{D}_{x}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] \right]</math>

Furthermore, the following relation applies:

<math display="block">{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] = {_{a}^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] - \sum\limits_{k = 0}^{\left\lfloor \alpha \right\rfloor}\left[ \frac{x^{k - \alpha}}{\Gamma\left( k - \alpha + 1 \right)} \cdot f^{\left( k \right)}\left( 0 \right) \right]</math>

where <math>{_{a}^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}</math> is the Riemann–Liouville fractional derivative.

=== Laplace transform ===
The [[Laplace transform]] of the Caputo-type fractional derivative is given by:

<math display="block">\mathcal{L}_{x}\left\{ {_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ f\left( x \right) \right] \right\}\left( s \right) = s^{\alpha} \cdot F\left( s \right) - \sum\limits_{k = 0}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - 1}\left[ s^{\alpha - k - 1} \cdot f^{\left( k \right)}\left( 0 \right) \right]</math>

where <math display="inline">\mathcal{L}_{x}\left\{ f\left( x \right) \right\}\left( s \right) = F\left( s \right)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sontakke |first1=Bhausaheb Rajba |last2=Shaikh |first2=Amjad |date=2015 |title=Properties of Caputo Operator and Its Applications to Linear Fractional Differential Equations |url=https://www.ijera.com/papers/Vol5_issue5/Part%20-%201/D505012227.pdf |journal=Journal of Engineering Research and Applications |volume=5 |issue=5 |pages=23–24 |issn=2248-9622}}</ref>

== Caputo fractional derivative of some functions ==
The Caputo fractional derivative of a constant <math>c</math> is given by:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ c \right] &= \frac{1}{\Gamma\left( \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha \right)} \cdot \int\limits_{a}^{x} \frac{\operatorname{D}_{t}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil}\left[ c \right]}{\left( x - t \right)^{\alpha + 1 - \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil}}\, \operatorname{d}t = \frac{1}{\Gamma\left( \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha \right)} \cdot \int\limits_{a}^{x} \frac{0}{\left( x - t \right)^{\alpha + 1 - \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil}}\, \operatorname{d}t\\
{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ c \right] &= 0
\end{align}</math>

The Caputo fractional derivative of a power function <math>x^{b}</math> is given by:<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Fractional Derivative |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FractionalDerivative.html |access-date=2024-05-20 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ x^{b} \right] &= {_{a}^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}_{x}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha}}\left[ \operatorname{D}_{x}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil}\left[ x^{b} \right] \right] = \frac{\Gamma\left( b + 1 \right)}{\Gamma\left( b - \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil  + 1 \right)} \cdot {_{a}^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}_{x}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha}}\left[ x^{b - \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil} \right]\\ {_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ x^{b} \right] &= \begin{cases} \frac{\Gamma\left( b + 1 \right)}{\Gamma\left( b - \alpha + 1 \right)} \left( x^{b - \alpha} - a^{b - \alpha} \right),\, &\text{for } \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - 1 < b \wedge b \in \mathbb{R}\\ 0,\, &\text{for } \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - 1 \geq b \wedge b \in \mathbb{N}\\ \end{cases}
\end{align}</math>

The Caputo fractional derivative of an [[exponential function]] <math>e^{a \cdot x}</math> is given by:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ e^{b \cdot x} \right] &= {_{a}^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}_{x}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha}}\left[ \operatorname{D}_{x}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil}\left[ e^{b \cdot x} \right] \right] = b^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil} \cdot {_{a}^{\text{RL}}\operatorname{I}_{x}^{\left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha}}\left[ e^{b \cdot x} \right]\\
{_{a}^{\text{C}}\operatorname{D}_{x}^{\alpha}}\left[ e^{b \cdot x} \right]  &= b^{\alpha} \cdot \left( E_{x}\left( \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha,\, b \right) - E_{a}\left( \left\lceil \alpha \right\rceil - \alpha,\, b \right) \right)\\
\end{align}</math>

where <math display="inline">E_{x}\left( \nu,\, a \right) = \frac{a^{-\nu} \cdot e^{a \cdot x} \cdot \gamma\left( \nu,\, a \cdot x \right)}{\Gamma\left( \nu \right)}</math> is the <math display="inline">\operatorname{E}_{t}</math>-function and <math display="inline">\gamma \left( a,\, b \right)</math> is the lower [[incomplete gamma function]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |date=2024 |title=E_t-Function |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ |access-date=2024-05-20 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>
